overview: Acjachemen communities belong to the landscape around San Juan Capistrano and surrounding parts of southern California. Juaneño is a mission-derived name. Their history connects independent villages, coastal and inland resources, colonial dispossession and continuing cultural life.

periods.title: Mission expansion and resistance
periods.summary: Mission San Juan Capistrano brought coercive labour, livestock expansion and disease. Acjachemen built mission structures while continuing ceremonies despite pressure to abandon them.

periods.title: Secularization and contested land
periods.summary: After the secularization act, Acjachemen sought irrigated mission lands. Formal titles were scarce; ranch encroachment continued, alongside family plots in the new San Juan pueblo.

periods.title: Dispossession and community connections
periods.summary: American occupation further undermined landholding. Families maintained connections with San Juan through work, residence and gatherings despite displacement and disease.

periods.title: Recovering language materials
periods.summary: The language project obtained Smithsonian materials in 1996 and began transferring words and phrases into a database, making archival knowledge available for community learning.

sections.title: Objects and evidence of everyday work

items.text: An Acjachemen basket from San Juan Capistrano, now Autry object 811.G.770, combines juncus wrapping with a bundled deergrass foundation. Black-dyed juncus supplies the design; sumac forms the starting coils. Bound ends and a tapered rim show the maker’s attention to a secure finish. The museum acquired it in 1937, but the record does not date its manufacture.

The mission museum identifies a grinding stone used to process acorns. It connects an everyday food to the work of breaking it down for preparation. The public description does not supply an excavation layer or manufacture date, so the stone cannot by itself establish when that practice began.

At Puhú in Black Star Canyon, animal remains studied by Tomczyk and Acebo indicate continued hunting of local mountain fauna during the colonial period. Their analysis found little or no contribution from livestock, challenging the story that residents depended on stolen animals before the reported 1832 massacre. Food waste provides evidence distinct from settlers’ accusations.

The Puhú researchers suggest that colonial ecological changes may have increased access to some native animals in this mountain setting. That is an interpretation, not proof that colonization benefited Indigenous people generally. Their work involved Tongva, Acjachemen and Payómkawichum collaborators; the village is not presented as exclusively one present-day community’s heritage.

Permanent villages and seasonal camps formed a connected landscape. The community history describes locally independent clans linked through marriage, exchange and ceremony. Chiefs worked with councils of Elders, making political and ceremonial responsibilities part of community life.

Culture bearer Heidi Harper Lucero describes growing basketry and food plants at home as urban development reduces gathering places. She also continues gathering juncus in ancestral locations. Her account links a finished basket to the longer work of tending plants and maintaining access to land.

Lucero describes bringing gifts when she gathers, collecting extra for Elders and giving elderberry jelly to others. Food gathering is therefore connected to obligations and generosity in her account. These are her documented practices as an Acjachemen and Ohlone person, rather than a rule assigned to every household.

Lucero also explains that permits and changing relationships with land managers can interrupt cultural work. Access renewed only for short periods fits poorly with activities requiring longer care. Her experience shows why preserving a technique involves relationships with places and institutions as well as teaching hand skills.

In 1996, the language project acquired film and tape materials held by the Smithsonian with foundation support and community donations. Organizers began copying words and phrases into a database. This was painstaking recovery of existing knowledge, not the creation of a new language.

Sonia Carmen worked through John Peabody Harrington’s field notes, prepared flash cards and shared recordings at language meetings. Archivist Lisa Woodward explains that the resulting collection includes pronunciation guidance and references back to source pages. Those references help learners trace an entry to its historical record.

Elder Jacque Nunez describes using online language materials to teach grandchildren while living away from the homeland. Rebecca Robles connects language with stories and spiritual traditions. Their accounts show that preservation includes ordinary family use and teaching, alongside museum collections and scholarly study.

ending.text: Acjachemen people continue to affirm their identity and teach their language and culture. Elder Rebecca Vallejo explicitly rejects the idea that colonization annihilated the people. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint is not a historical end date.
